propositions.text: The appellants appeal the Federal Court judgment dismissing their application under s. 6 of the PMNOC Regulations.
propositions.quote: Bristol-Myers Squibb & Gilead Sciences, LLC and Merck Sharp & Dohme Corp. (collectively, the appellants) appeal from the January 13, 2014 judgment of the Federal Court (2014 FC 30) dismissing their application made under s. 6 of the Patented Medicines (Notice of Compliance) Regulations, SOR/93-133 (PMNOC Regulations).

propositions.text: The appellants sought to prohibit the Minister from issuing a Notice of Compliance to Teva for a generic version of Atripla.
propositions.quote: In the application, the appellants sought an order prohibiting the Minister of Health from issuing a Notice of Compliance to Teva Canada Limited for a generic version of the appellants’ combination anti-retroviral medicine marketed under the brand name Atripla.

paragraphs.summary: The appellants appeal the Federal Court's dismissal of their application to prohibit the Minister from issuing a Notice of Compliance to Teva for a generic Atripla.

propositions.text: Teva asserted its product would not infringe the patent and alleged the patent is invalid in its NOA dated December 22, 2011.
propositions.quote: The appellants’ application was made in response to a Notice of Allegation (NOA) dated December 22, 2011, in which Teva asserted that its proposed product would not infringe Canadian Letters Patent 2,279,198, which is owned by Merck and licensed to the other appellants. Teva also alleged that the Patent is invalid.

paragraphs.summary: Teva alleged non-infringement and invalidity of the patent in its December 22, 2011 NOA, as found by the earlier decision-maker.

propositions.text: The Federal Court found appellants failed to prove on balance of probabilities that Teva tablets infringe the patent.
propositions.quote: The Federal Court found that the appellants had failed to prove on the balance of probabilities that the Teva tablets will infringe the Patent.

propositions.text: The Federal Court was not satisfied that Teva tablets contain Form I efavirenz claimed in the patent.
propositions.quote: Based on its assessment of the expert evidence, the Federal Court was not satisfied that the Teva tablets contain Form I efavirenz, the compound claimed in the Patent.

paragraphs.summary: The Federal Court found appellants failed to prove infringement and was not satisfied Teva tablets contain the patented compound.

propositions.text: The Federal Court found appellants' tests were unreliable proxies for Teva's manufacturing process due to various concerns.
propositions.quote: In particular, the Federal Court found that the appellants had failed to prove that the tests which they had conducted were a reliable proxy for the process Teva used to manufacture its tablets.

propositions.text: Concerns included lack of correspondence in grinding force, lack of particulars, failure of expert to observe tests, unnecessary heating steps, and missing excipients.
propositions.quote: Among other things, the Federal Court had concerns about: the lack of correspondence between the grinding force applied in the appellants’ tests and the force exerted by Teva’s process; the lack of particulars on the grinding force applied in the tests; the failure of the appellants’ expert to observe the tests; the addition of unnecessary heating steps into the tests; and the failure to include excipients into the testing material.

propositions.text: The Federal Court generally preferred Teva’s expert evidence over appellants'.
propositions.quote: In finding these facts, the Federal Court generally preferred the evidence of Teva’s expert over that of the appellants.

paragraphs.summary: The Federal Court found appellants' tests unreliable proxies and preferred Teva's expert evidence over appellants'.

propositions.text: Appellants raise two issues: improper evidentiary standard and failure to draw adverse inference against Teva.
propositions.quote: Before this Court, the appellants raise two issues. First, they submit that the Federal Court failed to apply the proper evidentiary standard. Second, they submit that the Federal Court failed to draw an adverse inference against Teva for refusing to produce its tablets to the appellants for testing.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argue the Federal Court erred on evidentiary standard and adverse inference against Teva.

propositions.text: The appeal involves questions of mixed fact and law and fact; standard of review is palpable and overriding error.
propositions.quote: Contrary to the appellants’ submission, this appeal does not raise extricable questions of law but, rather, questions of mixed fact and law suffused by fact, and questions of fact. Therefore, the appellants must demonstrate palpable and overriding error (Teva Canada Limited v. Novartis Pharmaceuticals Canada Inc., 2013 FCA 244 at paras. 10-12, 451 N.R. 246, Housen v. Nikolaisen, 2002 SCC 33, at paras. 10, 36, [2002] 2 S.C.R. 235).

paragraphs.summary: The court states the standard of review is palpable and overriding error for mixed fact and law questions.

propositions.text: The Federal Court did not err in finding appellants' testing methods unreliable and that infringement was not proven.
propositions.quote: In my view, the Federal Court committed no palpable and overriding error in concluding that the appellants’ testing methods were not a reliable proxy for Teva’s manufacturing process, and that as such, the appellants had not proven that the Teva tablets infringe.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no palpable error in Federal Court's conclusion that appellants' tests were unreliable and infringement unproven.

propositions.text: The Federal Court applied the correct burden of proof, balance of probabilities, and did not impose an impossible burden on appellants.
propositions.quote: As well, contrary to the appellants’ submission, the Federal Court judge applied throughout the correct burden of proof, the balance of probabilities (at para. 20). The Judge’s approach did not impose on the appellants a burden that was impossible to meet.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Federal Court correctly applied the balance of probabilities burden of proof.

propositions.text: Appellants argue Teva has initial burden to put allegations into play before appellants must prove allegations unjustified.
propositions.quote: At the hearing of this appeal, counsel for the appellants placed significant emphasis on one alleged error of the Federal Court in its application of the burden of proof. In particular, counsel stressed that in applications brought under s. 6 of the PMNOC Regulations, the second person (Teva) has an initial burden to put its allegations “into play” by presenting evidence sufficient to give them an air of reality. Counsel argued that it is only after this burden is met that the first person (the appellants) must prove, on the balance of probabilities, that the allegations are not justified (at paras. 31-32, appellants’ Memorandum of Fact and Law).

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argue Teva must initially put allegations into play before appellants prove allegations unjustified.

propositions.text: Appellants cite Pfizer case to support initial burden on second person to put allegations into play.
propositions.quote: In support of this argument, the appellants cited Pfizer Canada Inc. v. Apotex Inc., 2007 FC 26 at paragraphs 9, 12, [2007] F.C.J. No. 36 (QL), aff’d 2007 FCA 195, 367 N.R. 98.

propositions.text: Pfizer case's initial burden on second person applies only to invalidity allegations due to presumption of validity under Patent Act s. 43(2).
propositions.quote: However, in that case, the Federal Court’s finding that the second person must present evidence putting their allegations “into play” relates solely to allegations of invalidity. It was necessary for the Federal Court to make such a finding given the presumption of validity established by s. 43(2) of the Patent Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. P-4 – without any evidence from the second person, the legal position is that the patent is valid.

propositions.text: In non-infringement allegations, no presumption applies and no initial evidentiary burden on second person exists.
propositions.quote: However, in the case at bar, the allegation is non-infringement, not invalidity. There is no presumption in play and, thus, no initial onus on the second person to put forward evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains Pfizer applies only to invalidity allegations with presumption of validity; no initial burden exists for non-infringement allegations.

propositions.text: Once Teva alleged non-infringement in NOA, no further evidentiary burden on it existed; allegation was in play.
propositions.quote: Accordingly, I agree with Teva’s submission that once it alleged in its NOA that “[t]he Teva Product will not contain Form I nor is Form I used in the manufacture of the Teva Products” (Appeal Book, p. 53), there was no further evidentiary burden on it; its allegation of non-infringement was “in play.”

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees Teva's non-infringement allegation was in play once stated in NOA, with no further burden.

propositions.text: The court rejects appellants' submission that an adverse inference should be drawn against Teva for not producing tablets.
propositions.quote: I also reject the appellants’ submission that the Federal Court should have drawn an adverse inference against Teva for failing to produce its tablets.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects appellants' argument for adverse inference against Teva for non-production of tablets.

propositions.text: Federal Court found appellants better equipped to make compound for testing and Teva undertook not to assert tested material differed from Form Teva.
propositions.quote: In declining to draw an adverse inference, the Federal Court relied upon a number of facts before it. Among other things, it found that the appellants were “better equipped than most” to make the compound for testing purposes and could have done so (footnote to para. 24). Also, Teva undertook not to assert that the material obtained and tested by the appellants was different in character or composition from Form Teva.

paragraphs.summary: Federal Court found appellants better equipped to test and Teva undertook not to dispute tested material's similarity to Form Teva.

propositions.text: Production of tablets is not required under s. 6(7) of the PMNOC Regulations.
propositions.quote: The decision of the Federal Court judge not to draw an adverse inference is bolstered by the fact that production is not required under s. 6(7) of the PMNOC Regulations.

paragraphs.summary: Federal Court noted production is not required under PMNOC Regulations s. 6(7).

propositions.text: Appellants failed to demonstrate palpable and overriding error by Federal Court on adverse inference point.
propositions.quote: In my view, the appellants have failed to demonstrate any palpable and overriding error on the part of the Federal Court judge on this point.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes appellants failed to show palpable error on adverse inference issue.

propositions.text: The court would dismiss the appeal with costs.
propositions.quote: Therefore, for the foregoing reasons, I would dismiss the appeal, with costs.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the appeal with costs.
